summary: One spelling with two sides. The noun צָפוֹן is the north: the direction set against the south (נֶגֶב, תֵּימָן, דָּרוֹם), the north side of the Dwelling and the altar, the north wind, and above all “the land of the north”, from which Yahweh brought invaders on Jerusalem (Babylon, Jer 1:14–15) and from which he will gather Israel back (Jer 16:15); at the end Gog comes “from the recesses of the north” against the regathered land (Ezk 38:15). The verb צָפַן is to hide something to keep it, a child or a spy (Exo 2:2; Jos 2:4), or to store it up as treasure, Yahweh's words in the heart and his goodness for those who fear him (Psa 119:11; 31:20); intransitive, to lie hidden in ambush. Ugaritic, Aramaic and Phoenician share “north” (the holy mountain Ṣapan) with ṣ behind צ; whether “hide” is the same older root is not shown by any checked cognate.

words.summary: About 150 times, a third of them with the ending of direction (צָפֹנָה “northward”). It names the quarter of the world, the side of a building or a border, the wind, and the lands beyond Israel's north from which armies came down on it. Its cognates name the mountain Ṣapan north of Ugarit, and Psa 48:3 sets Mount Zion in “the recesses of the north”, so the word may first have been the mountain's name and then the direction it stood in; scripture uses it only as the direction and its lands.

senses.definition: The quarter of the world opposite the south, one of the four directions; with -ָה “northward”, with מִן “north of”. Used of the sides of the Dwelling, the altar, the temple, the camp and the borders of the land.

evidence.note: “Look צָפֹנָה וָנֶגְבָּה וָקֵדְמָה וָיָמָּה”: the four directions from where Abram stood.
Jacob's seed will spread “to the west and the east and the north and the south”.
“צָפוֹן וְיָמִין, you created them”: north set against the south (the right hand, facing east).
The wind “goes to the south (דָּרוֹם) and turns to the north”.
“Whether a tree falls to the south or to the north.”
Gatekeepers “to the four winds: east, west, north and south”.
“The second side of the Dwelling, on the north side (לִפְאַת צָפוֹן).”
The lampstand on the south side (תֵּימָנָה), “the table you shall put on the north side”.
The burnt offering slaughtered “on the side of the altar northward before Yahweh”.
The camp of Dan to the north of the tent of meeting.
“This shall be your north border.”
Israel camped “north of Ai (מִצְּפוֹן לָעַי)”.
Shiloh “north of Bethel”: a place located by direction.
The sea on twelve oxen, three facing north, three west, three south, three east.
“Lift your eyes the way of the north”: the image of jealousy north of the altar gate.
Dan's portion “from the north end”, the first of the tribes in Ezekiel's land.
The Mount of Olives split, “half of the mountain shall move northward and half southward”.
“He stretches out צָפוֹן over emptiness, and hangs the earth on nothing”: the northern sky.

senses.gloss: the north, the land of the north
senses.definition: The lands to Israel's north and beyond, “the land of the north” and its “recesses” (יַרְכְּתֵי צָפוֹן): the way invaders came, from Assyria and Babylon to Gog, and the country of Israel's exile from which Yahweh will bring them back.

evidence.note: “From the north the disaster shall be opened on all the inhabitants of the land.”
“All the families of the kingdoms of the north … shall set each his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem.”
“I will take all the families of the north … and Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant”: the north named.
“Evil looks down from the north, and great destruction.”
“A people comes from the land of the north, a great nation is stirred up from the recesses of the earth.”
“I will bring on Tyre Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the north.”
“He will stretch out his hand against the north and destroy Assyria.”
“A gadfly from the north” comes on Egypt; she is given “into the hand of the people of the north” (46:24).
Babylon in turn: “a nation comes up against her from the north.”
“From the north the destroyers shall come to her.”
“Smoke comes from the north” on Philistia.
“I have stirred up one from the north, and he has come”: Cyrus.
Gog: “You shall come from your place, from the recesses of the north, you and many peoples with you.”
“I will bring you up from the recesses of the north and bring you onto the mountains of Israel.”
“Beth Togarmah of the recesses of the north.”
“The princes of the north, all of them”, among the slain in the pit.
“At the time of the end … the king of the north shall storm against him” and enter the land of beauty (11:41).
“The king of the north” against “the king of the south” through Dan 11.
“Yahweh lives, who brought up the sons of Israel from the land of the north and from all the lands where he had driven them.”
“I bring them from the land of the north, and gather them from the recesses of the earth.”
Judah and Israel “come together from the land of the north to the land I gave your fathers”.
“Flee from the land of the north, says Yahweh.”
“I will say to the north, Give, and to the south, Do not keep back; bring my sons from far.”
“He gathered them out of the lands, from the east and the west, from the north and the sea.”
“Those going out to the land of the north have set my spirit at rest in the land of the north.”
“In the north by the river Euphrates they stumble and fall”: Carchemish.
“A storm wind came out of the north, a great cloud and fire.”
“They shall come from east and west, from north (βορρᾶ) and south, and recline in the kingdom of God”: the gathering of Psa 107:3 and Isa 49:12.

senses.gloss: the recesses of the north (a mountain)
senses.definition: The far north as the seat of a mountain: Mount Zion, “the city of the great king”, is “the recesses of the north”, and the king of Babylon boasts that he will sit on “the mountain of assembly in the recesses of the north”.

evidence.note: “Mount Zion, the recesses of the north (יַרְכְּתֵי צָפוֹן), the city of the great king.”
“I will sit on the mountain of assembly in the recesses of the north”: the boast of the king of Babylon (14:4).
“Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King”: the words of Psa 48:3.

senses.definition: The wind from the north, bringing rain or, in the garden of the Song, called up with the south wind to spread its scent.

evidence.note: “רוּחַ צָפוֹן brings forth rain.”
“Awake, צָפוֹן, and come, תֵימָן; blow on my garden.”
“Out of the north comes gold; with God is awesome majesty”: brightness from the northern sky.

evidence.locator: PSA 107:3 word 5, מִצָּפוֹן → βορρᾶ; ISA 49:12 word 7 and PSA 48:3 word 9 the same; βορρᾶς renders צָפוֹן ×84

evidence.note: “From east and west, from north and south”, gathering to the kingdom of God.
The city's gates: “from the north three gates”.

opposites.note: The south, set against north in directions and in “from south to north”; Daniel's “king of the south” against “the king of the north”.

evidence.note: “My sword shall go out against all flesh מִנֶּגֶב צָפוֹן.”

opposites.note: The south, with the south wind.
The right hand, the south to one facing east.

phrases.gloss: the recesses of the north, the far north

words.gloss: hide, keep hidden; store up, treasure; lie hidden, lurk
words.summary: Thirty times, mostly in Psalms, Proverbs and Job. What is hidden is kept: a child from Pharaoh, spies from the king of Jericho, the faithful in Yahweh's shelter, his words in the heart, goodness laid up for those who fear him. The wicked hide themselves to ambush. No checked cognate in another language means “hide”: those that share the root's letters mean “north”, so how “hide” and “north” belong together is not shown, and the verb's tie to the root rests on its own uses (the cognates listed with it are possible only).

stems.gloss: hide, keep hidden; store up, treasure; (intransitive) lie hidden, lurk

senses.definition: To hide a person so that he is kept from harm or from being found; of Yahweh, to hide his people in his shelter.

evidence.note: “She saw that he was good, and she hid him three months”; she could “hide him” no longer (2:3, hiphil).
Rahab “took the two men and hid them”.
“He will hide me (יִצְפְּנֵנִי) in his shelter in the day of trouble; he will conceal me (יַסְתִּרֵנִי) in the covert of his tent.”
“You hide them in the covert of your presence … you keep them (תִּצְפְּנֵם) in a shelter from the strife of tongues.”
“They conspire against צְפוּנֶיךָ”: Yahweh's hidden ones, his people, set in parallel with “your people”.
“These things you hid in your heart; I know that this was with you.”
“You have hidden their heart from understanding”: kept it from understanding.
“Whoever would hide her hides the wind”: to restrain a quarrelsome wife is to hold the wind.

senses.definition: To put something away and keep it as a store or treasure, for oneself or for another: commandments and words kept in the heart, wisdom and goodness laid up for the upright, and also guilt or sin kept for the reckoning.

evidence.note: “In my heart I have stored up your word, that I might not sin against you.”
“More than my portion I have treasured the words of his mouth.”
“If you receive my sayings and store up my commandments with you.”
“Keep (שְׁמֹר) my sayings and store up my commandments with you.”
“The wise store up knowledge.”
“He stores up sound wisdom for the upright.”
“How great is your goodness which you have stored up for those who fear you.”
“New and old choice fruits, my beloved, I have stored up for you.”
“The wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous.”
“They shall profane צְפוּנִי”: Yahweh's treasured place, the temple, entered by the violent.
“All darkness is laid up for his treasures (לִצְפוּנָיו).”
“With your treasure (צְפוּנְךָ) you fill their belly”: the reading of the text, whose written form is the noun צָפִין.
“The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up (צָרוּר); his sin is stored up (צְפוּנָה)”: kept for the reckoning.
“God stores up his iniquity for his sons.”

senses.definition: Without an object: to hide oneself in wait, of men who ambush the innocent.

evidence.note: “Let us lie in wait (נֶאֶרְבָה) for blood; let us lurk (נִצְפְּנָה) for the innocent without cause.”
“They lie in wait for their own blood; they lurk for their own lives.”
“He sits in ambush in the villages … his eyes watch in hiding (יִצְפֹּנוּ) for the helpless.”
“They gather, they hide (יִצְפֹּנוּ), they watch my steps.”

stems.gloss: be hidden; be stored up, reserved

senses.gloss: be hidden; be stored up, reserved
senses.definition: Passive of the qal: of iniquity, to be hidden from Yahweh's sight (it is not); of years and times, to be kept in store.

evidence.note: “They are not hidden (נִסְתְּרוּ) from my face, and their iniquity is not concealed (נִצְפַּן) from my eyes.”
“The number of years is stored up for the oppressor.”
“Why are times not stored up (set) by the Almighty?”

senses.definition: To hide someone away so as to keep him: the infant Moses, and Job in the grave until Yahweh's anger is past.

evidence.note: “She could no longer hide him (הַצְּפִינוֹ), and took for him an ark of papyrus.”
“Oh that you would hide me in the grave (בִּשְׁאוֹל תַּצְפִּנֵנִי), conceal me until your anger turns, appoint me a set time and remember me!”

evidence.locator: PSA 119:11 word 2, צָפַנְתִּי → ἔκρυψα; PSA 31:20 word 5, צָפַנְתָּ → ἔκρυψας; PSA 27:5 word 2, יִצְפְּנֵנִי → ἔκρυψεν; κρύπτω renders צָפַן ×6

evidence.note: “The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden (κεκρυμμένῳ) in a field”: the hidden thing that is a treasure.
“Your life is hidden (κέκρυπται) with Christ in God.”

parallels.note: Hide, conceal: Yahweh hides his own; iniquity is not hidden from him.
Lie in wait, with the intransitive “lurk”.
Keep: storing up commandments is keeping them.
Bind up: Ephraim's iniquity bound up, his sin stored up.
Hide, bury: darkness hidden for his treasures.

words.summary: Once, in Joel, of the invader from the north. Its other token (Num 26:15) is the clan name “the Zephonite”, from Zephon, a name filed under צפה.

senses.definition: The one from the north, the army Yahweh sends against his land and then drives out into a dry land, its front to the eastern sea and its rear to the western sea.

evidence.note: “I will remove far from you הַצְּפוֹנִי, and drive him into a land dry and desolate”: the army of 2:11, the locusts of 1:4 as an invader.

words.summary: Once, plural with a suffix: the things Esau had hidden away.

senses.definition: What has been put away and kept hidden, searched out by the plunderer.

evidence.note: “How Esau is searched out (נֶחְפְּשׂוּ), his hidden treasures (מַצְפֻּנָיו) sought out!”

words.summary: Only as the written text (Ketiv) of Psa 17:14, where the reading is the qal passive participle צְפוּנְךָ “your treasured thing”; it has no token of its own in the reading text.

senses.definition: A stored-up thing; Yahweh's store with which he fills the belly of men whose portion is in this life.

evidence.note: “With your treasure (Ketiv צְפִינְךָ) you fill their belly.”

words.gloss: Zaphon, a town of Gad in the Jordan valley
words.summary: A town given to Gad east of the Jordan, the same word as “north”. Its second token (Ezk 47:17) is the common noun “north”.

senses.definition: A town in the valley east of the Jordan, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon, given to Gad.

evidence.note: “In the valley, Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth and Zaphon.”
The Ephraimites “crossed over צָפוֹנָה” to Jephthah in Gilead: “northward”, or “to Zaphon”.

cognates.gloss: Ṣapan, the holy mountain north of Ugarit (Jebel al-Aqraʿ); its god; north
cognates.note: The mountain at the north border of Ugarit's kingdom, the seat of Baal (“Baal of Ṣapan”). Hebrew uses the name as the direction; Psa 48:3 sets Mount Zion in “the recesses of the north”, where Isa 14:13 puts the king of Babylon's “mountain of assembly”. Ugaritic ṣ shows ṣ behind צ.

evidence.note: “/ṣapan-/ (?) GN, holy mountain, bʿl ṣpn 1.109:9 ‘Baal of Ṣapan’ … also DN … il ṣpn 1.3:III:20 ‘the god Ṣapan’ (cf. H. ṣāpōn, Phoen. ṣpn).”
The kingdom of Ugarit “extended in the north to the area around Mount Ṣapan (classical Mons Casius, modern Jebel al-Aqraʿ)”.

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic, in the Targums for Hebrew צָפוֹן (Targ. Exo 26:20; Isa 14:13) and in the Talmud's rendering of Jer 46:20, “murderous peoples from the north”. Aramaic keeps צ for ṣ (it writes ט for ṯ̣ and ע for ṣ́), so it too shows ṣ behind צ.

evidence.note: “= h. צָפוֹן, north. Targ. Ex. XXVI, 20 … Targ. Is. XIV, 13 … Yoma 32ᵇ (transl. Jer. XLVI, 20) עממין קטולין מצ׳ murderous peoples from the north.”

cognates.note: Neo-Assyrian only, four times, so likely taken from the West Semitic word (Akkadian's own words for north are other); Akkadian writes ṣ for ṣ, ṣ́ and ṯ̣ alike, so it shows no sound.

evidence.note: “north” (×4; Neo-Assyrian).

cognates.gloss: Baal Ṣaphon, “Proprietor of Mount Ṣaphon”, a god; ṣpn in personal names
cognates.note: The same mountain name in Phoenician and Punic, as in Hebrew בַּעַל צְפוֹן, the place by the sea where Israel camped (Exo 14:2; Num 33:7).

evidence.note: “Baal/Proprietor of <Mount> Saphon, the god Baal as master of his divine mountain Ṣapon (Jabal al-Aqraʿ)”; KAI 50.2/3, “Baalsaphon and all the gods of Daphnae”; KAI 69.1, “Temple of Baalsaphon”.

cognates.gloss: hide (as listed; not checked in a Ugaritic dictionary)
cognates.note: Listed by Anderson and Moser under a reconstructed *ẓpn “hide”, with Hebrew צָפַן. If it stands, Ugaritic ẓ shows ṯ̣ behind צ for “hide” against ṣ for “north”: two older roots in one spelling. Not found in Segert's glossary; DULAT not consulted.

evidence.locator: SEM000548 ẓpn [hide] V, UGC004974 ẓpn [hide] V; HEB006385 ṣapan [hide] V

cognates.gloss: hide (as listed; not checked in Dillmann or Leslau)
cognates.note: Listed by Anderson and Moser under a separate *ṣpn “hide”. Ge'ez ṣ answers to ṣ or ṯ̣, so it would not decide between them. Not found in Dillmann's OCR text.

evidence.locator: SEM000919 ṣpn [hide] V, GEZ005467 ṣfn [hide] V

cognates.gloss: shelter (as listed; not in the Oracc glossaries, not checked in CAD)
cognates.note: Listed by Anderson and Moser with Ugaritic ẓpn and Hebrew צָפַן under *ẓpn “hide”. A shelter that hides would match Psa 27:5 and 31:21, but the word is unchecked.

doctrine.statement: Jeremiah was told at his call, “From the north the disaster shall be opened on all the inhabitants of the land”, and that the families of the kingdoms of the north would set their thrones at the gates of Jerusalem (Jer 1:14–15); later the families of the north are named, “Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant” (Jer 25:9), and he came with all his army and besieged the city (Jer 39:1). Ezekiel's vision of the glory came as a storm wind “out of the north” (Ezk 1:4), and Nebuchadnezzar is brought “from the north” on Tyre (Ezk 26:7). Babylon in turn falls to “a nation from the north” (Jer 50:3, 41; 51:48). Jesus foretold the next siege: “when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near” (Luk 21:20), and Rome's armies destroyed it in AD 70. Ezekiel then sees Gog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, come “from the recesses of the north” with many peoples “in the latter years”, against “a land brought back from the sword, gathered out of many peoples, on the mountains of Israel”, and fall there, so that the nations know Yahweh (Ezk 38:2, 8, 15–16; 39:2, 4, 7). Daniel's king of the north comes “at the time of the end” into the land of beauty, pitches his tents between the seas and the holy mountain, and comes to his end with none to help him; “at that time” Michael stands up, Daniel's people are delivered, and many who sleep in the dust awake (Dan 11:40–45; 12:1–2). After the thousand years Gog and Magog gather again against the camp of the saints and the beloved city, and fire from God consumes them (Rev 20:7–9). From the verses: the invader from the north is a pattern that recurs, Babylon in Jeremiah's day, Rome in AD 70, and Gog, the northern power (Russia), against the regathered nation of Israel at Christ's return, where Yahweh destroys him on the mountains of Israel; and each time it is Yahweh who brings the invader and Yahweh who judges him.

Jeremiah says the days are coming when men will no longer swear by Yahweh “who brought up the sons of Israel from the land of Egypt”, but “who brought up the sons of Israel from the land of the north and from all the lands where he had driven them”, “and I will bring them back to their land that I gave to their fathers” (Jer 16:14–15; 23:7–8). He sees the blind and the lame among them, “a great company” returning (Jer 31:8), and Judah and Israel coming “together from the land of the north to the land that I gave as an inheritance to your fathers” (Jer 3:18). Yahweh will say “to the north, Give”, and bring his sons from far (Isa 43:6). Jesus speaks of the same gathering: many will come “from east and west, from north and south, and recline in the kingdom of God” with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Luk 13:28–29). From the verses: the return from the north is a return to the land given to the fathers, a greater deliverance than the exodus, and it belongs with the kingdom of God on earth in which Abraham and his seed inherit the land.

Isaiah 14 is a proverb taken up “against the king of Babylon” (Isa 14:4). He said in his heart, “I will ascend to the heavens; above the stars of God I will raise my throne, and I will sit on the mountain of assembly in the recesses of the north” (Isa 14:13). The recesses of the north are where Psa 48:3 sets Mount Zion, “the city of the great king”, which Jesus calls Jerusalem (Mat 5:35): the king of Babylon meant to take the throne of Yahweh's own city. Instead he is brought down to the grave, to the recesses of the pit, and those who see him ask, “Is this the man who made the earth tremble, who shook kingdoms?” (Isa 14:15–16). From the verses: the one who would sit in the recesses of the north is a man, the king of Babylon, who died and went to the grave, not a fallen angel.

Job, having said that “man lies down and does not rise; till the heavens are no more they will not awake” (Job 14:12), asks, “Oh that you would hide me (תַּצְפִּנֵנִי) in the grave, that you would conceal me until your anger turns, that you would appoint me a set time and remember me!” (Job 14:13). He goes on, “If a man dies, shall he live? All the days of my service I will wait, until my change comes. You will call, and I will answer you” (Job 14:14–15). From the verses: the dead lie hidden in the grave, asleep and not conscious, until God remembers them and calls them; Job's hope is not a soul that lives on but being called out of the grave at God's set time.

note: Drafted 2026-11-18. Root key צפנ (BDB r.di.*). Assigned: r.di.ac צָפוֹן, r.di.aa צָפַן, r.di.ad צְפוֹנִי, r.di.ah מַצְפּוֹן with m.dd.ak (a zero-token cross-reference “מַצְפּוּנִים see צפן”), r.di.ab צָפִין (zero tokens; Ketiv of Psa 17:14), r.di.ae the town Zaphon; names in names/: r.di.ag zephaniah, a.dl.ba and a.dl.bv elizaphan (BDB files Elizaphan under אלה). Left out: צָפְנַת פַּעְנֵחַ (r.di.ai, with q.cf.ad), Joseph's Egyptian name (Gen 41:45), an Egyptian loan whose likeness to צפן is accidental; בַּעַל צְפוֹן (b.ci.al, r.di.af), filed under בעל, left for that root's entry, though it is “Baal of Ṣaphon” (see the Phoenician cognate); Zephon / Ziphion and the Zephonites (r.df.ac, r.df.ae, r.df.af), filed under צפה (“gaze”) and whose root is not clear, so no name file here. Shared tokens: Num 26:15 הַצְּפוֹנִי is counted under r.di.ad but is the clan name; Ezk 47:17 וְצָפוֹן is counted under the town r.di.ae but is “north”; Psa 17:14 and Psa 56:7 are not among the brief's verb tokens but read as qal forms. No Biblical Aramaic or Peshitta word: the Peshitta's north is ܓܪܒܝܐ. Arabic: صفن ḍfn/ẓfn tried by sound correspondence share no sense (صفن is of a horse standing on three legs) and are not recorded; Arabic has no cognate of either sense that was found. Open questions: (1) are “north” and “hide” one older root? North is ṣ by Ugaritic and Aramaic; hide has only Anderson and Moser's unverified Ugaritic ẓpn (ṯ̣) and Ge'ez ṣfn; check DULAT for ẓpn, Leslau for Ge'ez, CAD for ṣapānu, before calling it a split or tying “hide” to the root. The old explanation of north as “the hidden, dark region” is not evidenced and is not stated; the cognates suggest the direction is named from Mount Ṣapan. (2) The doctrine statements are reasoned conclusions to review: Gog as Russia at Christ's return, and Dan 11:40–45's king of the north “at the time of the end” read with Gog (data/prophecies.json treats Dan 11:2–35 as history and does not place 11:40–45); Joel's northerner is read as the invading army without dating it. (3) Jdg 12:1 צָפוֹנָה may be “to Zaphon” rather than “northward”. Leads not followed: Old South Arabian (Biella) for ṣpn; Krahmalkov's ṢPN personal names (p. 476).
